summary: Defines the Authentication-Results header field, which records the results of message authentication checks such as SPF and DKIM on an email message. Filters and mail clients can then use that. It was replaced by RFC 8601.

eli5.summary: A stamp on an email saying which security checks it passed.

subtitle: A header that tells mail software which authentication checks a message passed, such as SPF and DKIM.

tldr.problem: Mail servers check SPF, DKIM and other authentication methods, but downstream filters and mail clients need a common, machine-readable place to find the results.
tldr.mechanism: The Authentication-Results header field names the server that did the checking, then lists each method and its result, with optional properties showing what was evaluated. Servers add it at the top of the message and strip look-alike copies arriving from outside.
tldr.outcome: RFC 7601 obsoleted RFC 7001 and RFC 7410, and it has itself been obsoleted by RFC 8601.

today: RFC 7601 is a Standards Track document that obsoleted RFC 7001 and RFC 7410, and it was in turn obsoleted by RFC 8601, which is the current definition.

sections.title: Purpose and Trust Boundary
sections.content:
RFC 7601 specifies a header field called Authentication-Results that presents the results of message authentication in a machine-readable format. Its purpose is to give a Mail User Agent (MUA) and downstream filters a common place to find results so they can make filtering decisions or give users a recommendation about the origin of a message. It revises the original definition in RFC 5451, incorporating errata. End users are not expected to read it directly, and the document does not say how the data should be used.

The mere presence of the field does not mean its contents are valid; it reports assertions made by authentication schemes supposedly applied upstream. The field often has no integrity mechanism of its own, so it must be trusted implicitly, within a trust boundary that delimits the authority of an administrative management domain (ADMD). The document sets no requirement on MTAs to reject messages that fail checks.
sections.eli5: The note on a letter is only worth believing if it was written by someone in your own building.

sections.title: Format of the Header Field
sections.content:
The field is a structured header field and a trace field. Its value (after comments are removed) is an authentication identifier called authserv-id, an optional version, then statements of the form method=result, each optionally followed by a reason and by ptype.property=value items showing which part of the message was evaluated. A message can carry the field several times, or one field can hold several results. The special value none says no authentication was performed.

The ptype values are body, header, smtp and policy. SMTP commands are written in lowercase without spaces, so MAIL FROM becomes mailfrom. The authserv-id must be unique to the ADMD that produced it, and the common practice is to use the ADMD's DNS domain name. The version is 1, and a consumer that sees a version it does not know should stop parsing; for method versions, a result with an unsupported version SHOULD be ignored.
sections.eli5: Each stamp says who stamped it, then lists checks like 'signature: good' and 'sender address: good', plus what was looked at.

sections.title: Methods and Result Values
sections.content:
Each method returns one of a defined set of results. DKIM and DomainKeys share none, pass, fail, policy, neutral, temperror and permerror. SPF and Sender ID use the SPF results (none, pass, fail, softfail, neutral, temperror, permerror) plus policy. A policy result means local policy overrode the method's own answer, for example when SPF passes but the domain is on a local list of unacceptable domains.

The auth method reports SMTP AUTH, and the document also lists other registered methods such as vbr, dkim-adsp, rrvs and smime. It defines a new method, iprev, in which the client's IP address is looked up to get names (a PTR query), those names are looked up again to get addresses, and the test succeeds if the original address is among them. The number of names evaluated MUST be limited to protect the DNS. The RFC says this test is contentious and notes that its presence is not an endorsement.
sections.eli5: Each check gives a simple answer such as passed, failed, or could not be checked right now. There is also a special answer for 'it passed, but our own house rules say no'.

sections.title: Adding and Removing the Header Field
sections.content:
An MTA that does authentication adds the field, either once per test or once with all results, and MUST NOT add a result to an existing field. It SHOULD be inserted above other trace header fields so trusted fields are easy to spot, and it SHOULD NOT include data the method did not authenticate. If local policy treats a non-recoverable failure as grounds for rejection, the border MTA SHOULD reject at the SMTP level instead of adding the field, which avoids backscatter.

For security, an MTA MUST delete any instance of the field that claims, through its authserv-id, to have been added inside its trust boundary but did not come directly from a trusted MTA. This may require a list of known internal MTAs. MUAs and downstream filters SHOULD NOT interpret the field unless configured to, SHOULD only act on identifiers used within their own ADMD, MUST ignore unknown results, ptypes and unsupported methods, and SHOULD NOT reveal results to end users without careful design.
sections.eli5: The mail room throws away any fake stamps that arrive from outside, then adds its own real ones at the top of the letter.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The main risk is a forged field. A malicious sender can copy the receiving domain as the authserv-id and claim the message was authenticated; a non-conformant MTA would fail to strip it. For that reason processing should not be on by default. The document lists possible future fixes, such as signing the field with DKIM, but does not mandate one.

A pass does not make a message trustworthy, since spam can pass several methods. Other considerations include header reordering, denial-of-service through unbounded reverse lookups, backscatter, keeping the list of internal MTAs current, and attacks against the authentication methods themselves.
sections.eli5: A pass stamp only says the paperwork looked right. It does not promise the letter is friendly.

sections.title: Changes and Registries
sections.content:
IANA maintains registries for authentication methods, property types and result names, with new entries by Expert Review. This document gives a complete description of these registries, making it the authoritative definition, and marks the ADSP and DomainKeys entries as deprecated because their specifications are Historic.

Changes since RFC 7001 include applying RFC 7410, updating SPF references to RFC 7208, adding text on property values and SMTP AUTH results, fuller treatment of DomainKeys and Sender ID, and cleaner registry structure.
sections.eli5: There is an official list of allowed check names and answers, and this update tidied the list and retired two old entries.
